title: Flying Insect Detection and Classification with Inexpensive Sensors
protocol: Rear Culex tarsalis, Culex quinquefasciatus, Culex stigmatosoma, and Aedes aegypti adults from lab colonies originating from wild-caught individuals.
Raise mosquito larvae in enamel pans under standard laboratory conditions (27 °C, 16:8 hr light:dark [LD] cycle with 1 hr dusk/dawn periods).
Feed mosquito larvae ad libitum on a mixture of ground rodent chow and Brewer’s yeast (3:1, v:v).
Collect mosquito pupae into 200 ml cups.
Place collected pupae into experimental chambers or aspirate adult mosquitoes into experimental chambers within one week of emergence.
Ensure each experimental chamber contains 20 to 40 individuals of the same species/sex.
Feed adult mosquitoes ad libitum on a 10% sucrose and water mixture.
Replace food weekly.
Moisten cotton towels twice a week and place them on top of the experimental chambers to maintain humidity within the cage.
Place a 200 ml cup of tap water in the chamber at all times to help maintain overall humidity level.
Maintain the experimental chambers on a 16:8 hr light:dark [LD] cycle, 20.5-22 °C and 30-50% RH for the duration of the experiment.
Rear Musca domestica from a lab colony derived from wild-caught individuals.
Catch wild Drosophila simulans individuals and rear them in experimental chambers.
Rear Musca domestica larvae in plastic tubs under standard laboratory conditions (12:12 hr light:dark [LD] cycle, 26 °C, 40% RH) on a mixture of water, bran meal, alfalfa, yeast, and powdered milk.
Rear Drosophila simulans larvae in rearing chambers fed ad libitum with rotting fruit.
Aspirate adult Musca domestica into experimental chambers within one week of emergence.
Feed adult Musca domestica ad libitum on a mixture of sugar and low-fat dried milk, providing free access to water.
Feed adult Drosophila simulans ad libitum with rotting fruit.
Replace food weekly in the experimental chambers.
Maintain experimental chambers under 16:8 hr light:dark [LD] cycle conditions at 20.5-22 °C and 30-50% RH for experiment duration.
Construct an experimental chamber of either 67 cm L x 22 cm W x 24.75 cm H or 30 cm L x 20 cm W x 20 cm H.
Install a phototransistor array and a laser line in the chamber pointing at the phototransistor array.
Connect the phototransistor array to an electronic board.
Feed the output of the electronic board into a digital sound recorder.
Record the audio data as MP3 format.
Modify the lids of the experimental chambers by affixing a piece of mesh cloth inside to prevent insect escape.
Connect the experimental chamber to a power supply.
Turn on the power.
Find the laser lights and photoarray in the experimental chamber.
Align the laser lights to the photoarray.
Adjust the photoarray using magnets on the outside of the experimental chamber that correspond to magnets attached to the photoarray inside until the laser light is centered on all photodiodes.
Perform two sanity checks to ensure proper system setup.
Plug headphones into the audio jack.
Insert hand into and out of the experimental chamber near the photoarray.
Ensure laser light is visible when breaking its plane with the hand.
Listen for changes in noise level as hand moves through the beam.
Adjust photoarray if sound of movement is not audible.
Attach a thin piece of electrical wiring to an automatic toothbrush.
Turn on the toothbrush.
Plunge the wiring in and out of the experimental chamber near the phototray.
Ensure the laser light hits the piece of wiring as it moves.
If an audible change in frequency is detected when the wiring breaks the plane of laser light, proceed with data collection.
Re-align the laser lights and photoarray if no audible difference is detected.
Close the lid and add insects to the experimental chamber.
Turn on the recorder and make a voice annotation including species name, age of insects, date, time, ambient temperature, and relative humidity.
Pause the recording.
Connect the recorder to the system via an audio cable.
Resume the recording.
Record for 3 days, then stop the recording.
Download data from the recorder into a new folder on a PC.
Empty the recorder by deleting recorded data.
Repeat the recording process until no more than 5 insects are alive in the cage.
Use software to detect sounds produced by flying insects.
Run the detection software in MATLAB by typing “circandian_wbf (dataDir)” and pressing Enter, where dataDir is the directory of the recording data.
Wait until the algorithm terminates.
Check the detection results in the new folder named “dataDir_extf”.
Observe the example of a detected insect sound.
Extract a 1-second long audio clip centering at the current window from the recording.
Apply a digital filter to remove noise in the clip.
Save the filtered audio into the folder "dataDir_extf".
Save the occurrence time of the current window into the file "dataDir_time".
Move the sliding window to the point that immediately follows the extracted audio clip.
If the fundamental frequency is not within the range of 100 Hz to 1,200 Hz, move the sliding window 0.01 seconds forward.
Repeat the process until the sliding window reaches the end of the recording.
Compute the frequency spectrum of each insect sound using Discrete Fourier Transform (DFT).
Truncate the frequency spectrum to include only data points corresponding to the frequency range: 100 Hz to 2,000 Hz.
Use the truncated frequency spectrum in classification as the "representative" of the insect sound.
Train a Bayesian classifier.
Use the kNN density estimation approach to learn the posterior probability distribution using the sound feature.
Build a training dataset by randomly sampling insect sounds for each species.
Compute the truncated frequency spectrum for each sampled sound.
Compose the training dataset with the truncated spectrums and class labels (species name).
Compute the truncated frequency spectrum of an unknown insect sound.
Calculate the Euclidean distance between the truncated spectrum of the unknown object and all training data points.
Identify the top k nearest neighbors in the training dataset (k = 8).
Determine the posterior probability for each class based on the fraction of nearest neighbors labeled as that class.
Classify the unknown object to the class with the highest posterior probability.
Learn the circadian rhythm distributions for each species by analyzing sound occurrence times.
Obtain the occurrence time of insect sounds from detection results.
Build a histogram of occurrence times for each insect species.
Normalize the histogram so that the area of the histogram is one.
Classify an unknown insect sound by combining the insect sound with the circadian rhythm.
Obtain the probability of observing an insect of a specific class based on the circadian rhythm at the time the unknown sound occurred.
Compute the posterior probability that the unknown sound belongs to a specific class using the sound features as per section 4.1.2 steps.
Multiply the computed posterior probability by the obtained probability from the circadian rhythm.
Classify the unknown sound to the class with the highest new posterior probability.
Add one more feature to the classifier: insect geographic distribution.
Learn the geographic distribution of the species from historical records or literature.
Gather first-hand knowledge about the species' geographic distribution from field technicians/biologists if available.
Simulate a graphic representation of the species' geographic distribution for demonstration purposes.
Classify an "unknown insect sound" using "flying sound" and two additional features.
Compute the probability of observing an insect from a specific class at the location where the sound was intercepted.
Calculate the posterior probability that the "unknown sound" belongs to a class based on sound features and circadian rhythms.
Multiply the calculated posterior probability by the previously computed probability.
Classify the "unknown sound" into the class with the highest new posterior probability after multiplication.
In the training phase, learn the class-conditioned density functions of new features for the classifier.
Compute the probability of observing the feature in each class using the density functions learned previously.
Multiply this probability with the previous posterior probability corresponding to the "unknown sound" belonging to each class.
Classify the unknown object to the class that has the highest new posterior probability.
